etymology: Hebrew Gemaryah (H1587), the LORD has accomplished or the LORD has completed — from gamar (H1584), to end, to complete, to perfect, and Yah, the covenant name.
biblical_def: Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe was one of the princes of Judah in Jehoiakim's reign, and he behaved well in a court that did not. It was his chamber in the higher court of the LORD's house that Baruch used to read Jeremiah's roll in the ears of all the people (Jer 36:10). His son Michaiah heard the reading and carried word of it down to the princes in the scribe's chamber (Jer 36:11-12). And when the roll had been brought to Jehoiakim and the king began cutting it up leaf by leaf and feeding it to the hearth, three men tried to stop him: Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them (Jer 36:25). They failed. A second Gemariah, son of Hilkiah, was one of the two envoys Zedekiah sent to Babylon who carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jer 29:3). The house of Shaphan runs through the whole period as the family that kept sheltering the prophets, and Gemariah is one of its better members.
webster_summary: A prince of Judah under Jehoiakim, son of Shaphan the scribe, in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's roll and who pleaded with the king not to burn it.
webster_full: GEMARIAH, Hebrew Gemaryah, the LORD has accomplished.
1. Son of Shaphan the scribe, a prince of Judah in the reign of Jehoiakim.
Baruch read the words of Jeremiah in his chamber in the house of the LORD.
He was one of three who made intercession that the king would not burn the roll.
2. Son of Hilkiah, sent by Zedekiah to Babylon, who carried Jeremiah's letter to the captives.
scriptures: Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the LORD'S house, in the ears of all the people.
When Michaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the words of the LORD,

Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them.
corruption_summary: Faithfulness is measured by whether it succeeded; Gemariah pleaded, was refused, and is named in Scripture for the pleading.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Gemariah is uncontested. The pressure he applies is on our way of scoring obedience. Three princes stood up in a royal chamber and asked the king not to burn the word of God. The king burned it anyway, and then sent to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah. By every outcome-based measure the intercession accomplished nothing: the roll went into the fire leaf by leaf while they watched.

The Holy Ghost saw fit to record their names anyway, and to record them as the men who tried. That is how Scripture usually scores things. It is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful (1Co 4:2) — faithful, not successful. Noah preached a hundred and twenty years and saved eight people. Jeremiah preached forty and saw the city burn. And the roll itself outlived the fire: God simply told Jeremiah to take another roll and write all the former words, and there were added besides unto them many like words (Jer 36:32). The principle to recover is that the obligation is to speak, and the outcome belongs to God, who is perfectly capable of replacing what a king can burn.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gemaryah (H1587), from gamar (H1584), to complete, to accomplish, with Yah.
roots_lines: Hebrew gamar (H1584) — to end, complete, accomplish; the LORD will perfect that which concerneth me (Psa 138:8).
Hebrew Gemaryah (H1587) — son of Shaphan (Jer 36:10-25) and son of Hilkiah (Jer 29:3).
Hebrew Shaphan (H8227) — Shaphan the scribe, who read the book of the law to Josiah; head of a house that sheltered prophets.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a scroll; the roll Jehoiakim burned.
Hebrew paga (H6293) — to make intercession, to entreat; what the three princes did before the king.
usage: “In the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe”.
“Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king”.
“But he would not hear them”.

etymology: Hebrew Yehudi (H3065), a Jew or a man of Judah — the ordinary gentilic used as a personal name; his great-grandfather is called Cushi, an Ethiopian name.
biblical_def: Jehudi the son of Nethaniah appears in one chapter and does one thing, and it is among the worst deeds recorded of a servant in Scripture. The princes first sent him to fetch Baruch and the roll so that they could hear it for themselves (Jer 36:14). Then the king sent him to fetch the roll from Elishama's chamber, and Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king (Jer 36:21). It was winter, and there was a fire on the hearth. And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed (Jer 36:23). The knife in the hand is Jehoiakim's by command, and the text keeps the responsibility at the throne; but the hand that read the word of God aloud and then cut it up was Jehudi's. His name means simply a Jew. The man named for the covenant people destroyed the covenant word, three or four leaves at a time, and neither the king nor his servants were afraid, nor rent their garments (Jer 36:24).
webster_summary: The officer of Jehoiakim who read Jeremiah's roll before the king and cut it with a penknife into the fire; his name means a Jew.
webster_full: JEHUDI, Hebrew Yehudi, a Jew, a man of Judah.
Son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi.
Sent by the princes to fetch Baruch and the roll of Jeremiah's words.
Sent by the king to fetch the roll out of Elishama the scribe's chamber, and he read it before the king.
When he had read three or four leaves he cut it with the penknife and cast it into the fire.
scriptures: Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them.

So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Obeying orders is offered as a defence; Jehudi read the word of God aloud and then cut it up, and Scripture records his name.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 36 puts two kinds of servant in the same room. Three princes asked the king to stop and were refused. One officer took the penknife. The king is the one the chapter condemns most heavily — the sentence against Jehoiakim is that he should have none to sit upon the throne of David and his dead body cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night (Jer 36:30). But the text does not let the instrument disappear into the command. It names him, twice, and tells us exactly what he did with his hands.

Scripture nowhere accepts the plea that a man was only carrying out instructions. We ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29) is the rule where the two conflict; Saul's footmen refused to fall on the priests of the LORD at his order, and their refusal is recorded to their credit (1Sa 22:17); the midwives of Egypt disobeyed Pharaoh and God dealt well with them (Exo 1:17-20). The principle to recover is that lawful authority is real and is to be honoured, and that its writ stops precisely where it commands what God forbids. Every man answers for his own hands, and the fact that someone senior wanted it done has never once been a defence at the bar of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yehudi (H3065), a Jew, a man of Judah; used here as a personal name.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yehudi (H3065) — the officer of Jehoiakim; Jeremiah 36:14, 36:21, 36:23.
Hebrew Yehudah (H3063) — Judah, praise; the tribe and kingdom from which the gentilic comes.
Hebrew taar (H8593) — a knife, a razor; he cut it with the penknife (Jer 36:23).
Hebrew ach (H254) — a fire-pot, a hearth; the brazier burning before the king in the winter house.
Hebrew qara (H7167) — to rend, to tear; yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments (Jer 36:24).
usage: “All the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah… unto Baruch”.
“And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king”.
“He cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth”.

etymology: Hebrew Yaazanyah (H2970), the LORD hears or whom the LORD hearkens to — from azan (H238), to give ear, to listen, and Yah, the covenant name.
biblical_def: Four men bear this name, and two of them stand at opposite poles of the last generation of Judah. The first is Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habaziniah, head of the Rechabites, whom the prophet set before pots of wine in a chamber of the LORD's house and invited to drink (Jer 35:3). They refused, because Jonadab their father had commanded them not to drink wine, nor build houses, nor sow seed, and they had kept his word for generations — and the LORD made their obedience a public rebuke of Judah's. The second is Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, whom Ezekiel saw in vision in a chamber of the temple, standing in the midst of seventy of the ancients of Israel with a censer in his hand, a thick cloud of incense going up before pictures of creeping things portrayed upon the wall (Eze 8:11). Two men, both named the LORD hears: one keeping a family rule for centuries at cost, and one burning incense to idols in the dark, saying the LORD seeth us not.
webster_summary: The name of four men, chiefly the head of the Rechabites whom Jeremiah tested, and the son of Shaphan whom Ezekiel saw offering incense to idols.
webster_full: JAAZANIAH, Hebrew Yaazanyah, the LORD hears.
1. Son of Jeremiah, head of the house of the Rechabites, who refused the wine Jeremiah set before them.
Their obedience to Jonadab their father was made a rebuke of Judah's disobedience to God.
2. Son of Shaphan, seen by Ezekiel with a censer among seventy ancients before idols on the wall.
3. A prince of the people seen at the east gate. 4. A captain who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah.
scriptures: Jer 35:3
Then I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habaziniah, and his brethren, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites;
Eze 8:11

And there stood before them seventy men of the ancients of the house of Israel, and in the midst of them stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, with every man his censer in his hand; and a thick cloud of incense went up.
Eze 11:1

Moreover the spirit lifted me up, and brought me unto the east gate of the LORD'S house, which looketh eastward: and behold at the door of the gate five and twenty men; among whom I saw Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.

And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.
corruption_summary: Private religion is assumed to be unseen; Ezekiel was shown the elders of Israel at their secret worship and told to look again.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 8 is the vision of what Judah's leaders were doing where nobody could watch. The prophet is brought to a door, told to dig through the wall, and shown a chamber painted with creeping things and abominable beasts, seventy elders in the dark with censers, and Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing in the middle. Then the LORD gives their reasoning: Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth (Eze 8:12). The men burning the incense had concluded that God was not looking.

The chamber of imagery is a good name for what the age has industrialised. Screens deliver, in private, exactly what Ezekiel was shown behind a wall, and the same sentence is whispered over it: nobody sees. Scripture answers with the plainest of facts — all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13), and be sure your sin will find you out (Num 32:23). The principle to recover is that there is no private life before God, that secret religion is the truest measure of a man, and that the elders of Israel were ruined not by what they did in the temple court but by what they did in the room behind it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yaazanyah (H2970), from azan (H238), to give ear, with Yah, the covenant name.
roots_lines: Hebrew azan (H238) — to give ear, to listen attentively; Give ear, O my people, to my law (Psa 78:1).
Hebrew Yaazanyah (H2970) — borne by four men; Jeremiah 35:3, Ezekiel 8:11, 11:1, 2 Kings 25:23.
Hebrew Rekab (H7394) — Rechab, whose son Jonadab bound his house to a rule they kept for generations.
Hebrew maskith (H4906) — imagery, a figured stone or picture; the chambers of his imagery (Eze 8:12).
Hebrew miqtereth (H4730) — a censer; the vessel in the hand of each of the seventy.
usage: “Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah… and the whole house of the Rechabites”.
“In the midst of them stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, with every man his censer in his hand”.
“The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth” (Eze 8:12).

etymology: Hebrew Chanamel (H2601), God is gracious — from chanan (H2603), to be gracious, and El (H410), God.
biblical_def: Hanameel was Jeremiah's cousin, and he is the other party to the strangest property transaction in the Bible. Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians, the country was overrun, the prophet himself was shut up in the court of the prison for telling the king the city would fall — and the LORD told him his cousin was coming to sell him a field. Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it (Jer 32:7). He came, exactly as foretold, and Jeremiah says Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD (Jer 32:8). So the prophet bought farmland in a district already in enemy hands, weighed out seventeen shekels of silver, signed the evidence, sealed it, called witnesses, and had Baruch put the deeds in an earthen vessel that they may continue many days (Jer 32:14). The reason is given in the next verse: Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land (Jer 32:15). It was a prophecy performed with a title deed.
webster_summary: Jeremiah's cousin, who sold him a field in Anathoth during the siege of Jerusalem as a sign that the land would be possessed again.
webster_full: HANAMEEL, Hebrew Chanamel, God is gracious.
The son of Shallum, Jeremiah's uncle; therefore the prophet's cousin.
He came to Jeremiah in the court of the prison during the Babylonian siege.
He offered his field in Anathoth, the right of redemption being Jeremiah's.
Jeremiah bought it for seventeen shekels of silver and sealed the evidence in an earthen vessel.
scriptures: Jer 32:7
Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it.
Jer 32:8

So Hanameel mine uncle's son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the LORD, and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that is in Anathoth, which is in the country of Benjamin: for the right of inheritance is thine, and the redemption is thine; buy it for thyself. Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
Jer 32:9
And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver.

And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison.
corruption_summary: Hope is treated as a mood; Jeremiah's hope was a legal document, witnessed, sealed and stored for a future he would not see.
corruption_paragraphs: Biblical hope is routinely confused with optimism — a temperament, a way of looking on the bright side, a feeling that things will probably work out. Jeremiah had no such feeling and every reason not to. He had preached the fall of the city for forty years, he was in custody for preaching it, and the Chaldean siege works were going up outside the wall as his cousin walked in. He did not say that things might not be as bad as they looked. He said the city would certainly fall, and then he bought a field in the occupied territory and paid for it in silver.

That is what hope is in Scripture: confidence in a promise, acted on at cost, about a future the man himself may not live to see. Abraham looked for a city which hath foundations; Moses esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward (Heb 11:26). And the deeds went into an earthen vessel to last, because the word was Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land. The principle to recover is that Christian hope is evidenced by what a believer is willing to spend on God's word about a future he cannot see from here.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chanamel (H2601), from chanan (H2603), to be gracious, with El (H410), God.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to be gracious, to show favour; the root of Hanameel, Hannah, Hananiah and John.
Hebrew Chanamel (H2601) — Jeremiah's cousin; Jeremiah 32:7, 32:8, 32:9, 32:12.
Hebrew geullah (H1353) — the right of redemption, the kinsman's duty to buy back family land (Lev 25:25).
Hebrew Anathoth (H6068) — Anathoth, the priestly town in Benjamin where Jeremiah was born.
Hebrew sepher hammiqnah — the book of the purchase, the sealed deed placed in an earthen vessel.
usage: “Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it”.
“Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD”.
“Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land” (Jer 32:15).

etymology: Hebrew Achiman (H289), commonly read brother of a gift or my brother is a gift — from ach (H251), brother, with a second element read as man, a portion or gift.
biblical_def: Ahiman was one of the three sons of Anak at Hebron, the giants whose presence broke the nerve of the ten spies. And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were (Num 13:22). The report that followed described a land that ate up its inhabitants, and men beside whom the spies were as grasshoppers in their own sight. Caleb alone said Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it (Num 13:30) — and forty-five years later, an old man of eighty-five, he asked for that mountain and got it: Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai (Jos 15:14). Judges records the same conquest from the tribe's side (Jdg 1:10). A second Ahiman is a porter of the house of God in the register of those who dwelt at Jerusalem (1Ch 9:17). The giant of Hebron is the standing biblical example of an obstacle that is real, that is correctly measured, and that is nevertheless beaten at the appointed time by a man who believed God about it.
webster_summary: One of the three sons of Anak at Hebron, the giants who terrified the spies and were afterwards driven out by Caleb; also a porter after the captivity.
webster_full: AHIMAN, Hebrew Achiman, commonly read brother of a gift.
1. One of the three sons of Anak dwelling at Hebron when the spies came.
Named with Sheshai and Talmai, the children of Anak.
Caleb drove the three sons of Anak from Hebron forty-five years later.
2. A porter of the house of God among those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity.
scriptures: And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)
And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
Jdg 1:10
And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai.
And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;
corruption_summary: Faith is presented as refusing to see the difficulty; Caleb saw the giants exactly as the other spies did, and drew the opposite conclusion.
corruption_paragraphs: A shallow account of faith makes it a kind of selective blindness — a determination not to look at the obstacle, to speak only positively, to deny the size of the giants. Numbers 13 will not support it. Caleb and Joshua walked the same forty days as the other ten, saw the same walled cities and the same sons of Anak at Hebron, and never once disputed the report of what was there. The difference was not in the survey. It was in a single omitted factor: the LORD is with us: fear them not (Num 14:9).

That is the shape of biblical faith everywhere. It counts the cost (Luk 14:28), it does not pretend the furnace is cool or the lions toothless, and it adds God to the arithmetic as the largest term. Caleb was eighty-five when he came back for Hebron and asked for the hardest ground in the inheritance, saying if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out (Jos 14:12). The principle to recover is that faith is realism with God included, and that the believer who has told himself the difficulty is smaller than it is has not exercised faith but avoided it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Achiman (H289), from ach (H251), brother, with a second element signifying a portion or gift.
roots_lines: Hebrew Achiman (H289) — a son of Anak (Num 13:22) and a porter after the captivity (1Ch 9:17).
Hebrew Anaq (H6061) — Anak, whose sons were the giants of Hebron; the children of Anak, which come of the giants (Num 13:33).
Hebrew nephilim (H5303) — giants, fallen ones; the word in the spies' report.
Hebrew Chebron (H2275) — Hebron, formerly Kirjath-arba, the city Caleb asked for and took.
Hebrew malé acharey — to follow fully; he hath wholly followed the LORD (Num 32:12), said of Caleb.
usage: “Where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were”.
“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak”.
“Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it” (Num 13:30).

etymology: Hebrew Kenaanah (H3668), a form of Kenaan, Canaan — merchant or trafficker, from a root meaning to bend or bring low.
biblical_def: Chenaanah is chiefly remembered as the father of Zedekiah, the leading court prophet of Ahab. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat sat in their robes at the gate of Samaria and four hundred prophets promised victory at Ramoth-gilead, Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them (1Ki 22:11; 2Ch 18:10). It was a prophetic sign-act, performed with the right formula and the right props, and it was a lie. When Micaiah at last told the truth and was ordered to prison on bread and water, Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee? (1Ki 22:24). Ahab went to Ramoth-gilead in disguise and was killed by an arrow shot at a venture. A second Chenaanah is a son of Bilhan in the genealogy of Benjamin (1Ch 7:10).
webster_summary: Father of Zedekiah, the false prophet who made horns of iron and smote Micaiah; also a Benjamite in the genealogy of Bilhan.
webster_full: CHENAANAH, Hebrew Kenaanah, a form of Canaan, merchant or trafficker.
1. Father of Zedekiah, chief of the four hundred prophets of Ahab.
His son made horns of iron and promised Ahab victory at Ramoth-gilead.
He smote Micaiah the prophet on the cheek for contradicting him.
2. A son of Bilhan, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin.
scriptures: And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them.
But Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?
And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah had made him horns of iron, and said, Thus saith the LORD, With these thou shalt push Syria until they be consumed.
The sons also of Jediael; Bilhan: and the sons of Bilhan; Jeush, and Benjamin, and Ehud, and Chenaanah, and Zethan, and Tharshish, and Ahishahar.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is authenticated by confidence and consensus; four hundred agreed, one man was right, and the test Scripture gives is the word itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Everything about Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah looked right. He had the formula — Thus saith the LORD. He had a sign-act with iron horns, drawn from Moses' blessing on Joseph. He had four hundred colleagues saying the same thing, the king's confidence, and the boldness to strike a dissenter in public. Micaiah had none of it: one man, a reputation for never prophesying good concerning Ahab, and a sentence of prison. The count was four hundred to one, and the one was right.

Scripture never allows numbers, confidence or spiritual manner to authenticate a message. The tests are the content and the outcome: a prophet who calls after other gods is to be rejected even if his sign comes to pass (Deu 13:1-3), and a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the LORD (Deu 18:22). To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them (Isa 8:20). This is the whole ground for testing every modern claim to a fresh word, and for the cessationist conviction this dictionary holds: the canon is closed, and the church is not at the mercy of whoever sounds most certain. The principle to recover is that Micaiah's answer — what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak (1Ki 22:14) — is the only qualification that has ever mattered.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kenaanah (H3668), from Kenaan (H3667), Canaan, a merchant or trafficker.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kenaan (H3667) — Canaan; the word also means a merchant or trafficker.
Hebrew Kenaanah (H3668) — father of Zedekiah the false prophet (1Ki 22:11), and a Benjamite (1Ch 7:10).
Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn, an emblem of strength; the iron horns Zedekiah made.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets (1Ki 22:22).
Hebrew Mikayehu (H4321) — Micaiah, who is like the LORD; the one true prophet in the room.
usage: “Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron”.
“Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?”
“What the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak” (1Ki 22:14).

etymology: Hebrew Chaggith (H2294), festive or born on a feast day — from chag (H2282), a feast, a festival, a solemn appointed gathering.
biblical_def: Haggith was one of David's wives at Hebron and the mother of Adonijah, his fourth son (2Sa 3:4; 1Ch 3:2). Scripture never records a word of hers, and yet it names her five times, because it will not let Adonijah be spoken of without her: Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king (1Ki 1:5); Adonijah the son of Haggith doth reign, and David our lord knoweth it not (1Ki 1:11); Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon (1Ki 2:13). The repetition is deliberate, because the whole crisis of the succession is a contest between two mothers' sons, and the narrative keeps the houses visible. Of Adonijah himself the text gives the diagnosis in a single line: his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so? (1Ki 1:6). He was a goodly man, never corrected, and he tried to take the kingdom. Her name means festive, born at a feast. The son born in a season of rejoicing died by Solomon's order after one request too many.
webster_summary: A wife of David at Hebron and the mother of Adonijah, who exalted himself to be king; her name means festive.

corruption_summary: Correction is treated as damaging to a child; Scripture gives the uncorrected son as the explanation of the rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: First Kings 1:6 is one of the most quietly devastating verses about parenting in the Bible. Explaining how Adonijah came to attempt a coup against his own dying father, the text says: And his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so? and he also was a very goodly man. Two facts, set side by side. He was handsome and impressive; and no one had ever asked him to account for anything. David, who had buried Amnon and Absalom under the same failure, had learned nothing in time to save this son.

The prevailing view holds that correction wounds a child's spirit and that the loving parent affirms rather than restrains. Scripture's judgment is the reverse, and it is blunt: He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes (Pro 13:24); the rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame (Pro 29:15). Eli's house fell for the same reason — his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not (1Sa 3:13). The principle to recover is that the question why hast thou done so? is an act of love, and that a parent who cannot bring himself to displease his child has chosen his own comfort over the child's soul.

etymology: Hebrew Azubah (H5806), forsaken — the passive participle of azab (H5800), to leave, to loose, to forsake; the same word Isaiah reverses in Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken (Isa 62:4).
biblical_def: Two women bear this name. The first is a wife of Caleb the son of Hezron, who bore him Jesher and Shobab and Ardon, and after whose death Caleb took Ephrath, who bore him Hur (1Ch 2:18-19). The second is the mother of one of Judah's best kings: Jehoshaphat was thirty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi (1Ki 22:42; 2Ch 20:31). The books of Kings and Chronicles name the queen mother of every king of Judah, good and bad, as a fixed part of the formula — a small standing testimony to the weight Scripture gives to the woman who raised him. Azubah's name means forsaken, which is a hard thing to carry; and yet it is precisely this word that God takes up and overturns when He describes the restoration of His people: Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate… for the LORD delighteth in thee (Isa 62:4).
webster_summary: The name of two women: a wife of Caleb the son of Hezron, and the mother of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. It means forsaken.
webster_full: AZUBAH, Hebrew Azubah, forsaken; from azab, to forsake.
1. A wife of Caleb the son of Hezron, mother of Jesher, Shobab and Ardon.
After her death Caleb took Ephrath, who bare him Hur.
2. The daughter of Shilhi, and mother of Jehoshaphat king of Judah.
The name of the queen mother is recorded for every king of Judah.
scriptures: Jehoshaphat was thirty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.

And Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah: he was thirty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.
And Caleb the son of Hezron begat children of Azubah his wife, and of Jerioth: her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon.
And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur.
corruption_summary: God's people are told that a sense of abandonment is the truth about their case; Scripture takes the word Forsaken and cancels it.
corruption_paragraphs: The feeling of being forsaken by God is one of the commonest experiences in the believing life and one of the least reliable witnesses to the facts. The Psalms are full of it — My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? (Psa 22:1), Why standest thou afar off, O LORD? (Psa 10:1) — and Scripture never rebukes the men who said so. It simply refuses to let the feeling have the last word. Zion said The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me, and the answer came: Can a woman forget her sucking child…? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands (Isa 49:14-16).

The reason the promise holds is that the forsaking happened, once, to Someone else. Psalm 22:1 is the cry the Lord Jesus made from the cross, and He was in fact forsaken there, in the dark, bearing wrath, so that the promise to His people could be I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Heb 13:5). The principle to recover is that a Christian's sense of abandonment, however severe, is a symptom and not a verdict; the name Azubah is one God has publicly revoked — thou shalt be called Hephzibah… for the LORD delighteth in thee (Isa 62:4).

etymology: Hebrew Motsa (H4162), a going forth, an outgoing, a spring of water — from yatsa (H3318), to go out, to come forth.
biblical_def: Two men bear this name. The first is a son of Caleb by his concubine Ephah, in the genealogy of Judah: And Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bare Haran, and Moza, and Gazez (1Ch 2:46). The second is a link in the long Benjamite line that carries the house of Saul forward after Gilboa: Zimri begat Moza, and Moza begat Binea, and after Binea came Rapha, Eleasah and Azel (1Ch 8:36-37; 9:42-43). The name means a going forth, from yatsa, and the noun is used for the rising of the sun, for the spring where water comes out of the rock, and for the utterance that proceeds from a mouth. Scripture uses it in two of its greatest sentences. One is Moses' word in the wilderness, quoted by the Lord Jesus against the tempter: man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live (Deu 8:3). The other is Micah's prophecy of Bethlehem, of the Ruler whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting (Mic 5:2).
webster_summary: The name of two men: a son of Caleb by Ephah his concubine, and a Benjamite in the line of Saul's house. It means a going forth.
webster_full: MOZA, Hebrew Motsa, a going forth, an outgoing, a spring.
1. A son of Caleb by Ephah his concubine, in the genealogy of Judah.
2. A Benjamite, son of Zimri, in the line descending from Saul and Jonathan.
His son was Binea, and after him Rapha, Eleasah and Azel.
From yatsa, to go out or come forth.
scriptures: And Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bare Haran, and Moza, and Gazez: and Haran begat Gazez.

And Moza begat Binea: Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what proceeds out of the mouth of God is the food a man actually lives on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Moza is uncontested. The word his name is built on carries a claim the age is organised to deny. Motsa is what comes out — the water out of the rock, the sun out of its chamber, the word out of the mouth — and Deuteronomy uses it to say where a man's life comes from: man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live (Deu 8:3).

The Lord Jesus quoted that sentence in the wilderness after forty days without food, to a tempter who was proposing bread. He was not denying that bread is necessary; He had made it, and He fed thousands with it. He was denying that bread is sufficient, and denying it at the moment when hunger made the point hardest to hold. A culture that has solved bread and cannot tell why its people are starving has run the experiment. The principle to recover is that Scripture is not a supplement to a life otherwise sustained; it is the ration. Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart (Jer 15:16).

etymology: Hebrew Beker (H1071), a young camel or firstborn — from bakar (H1069), to bear early fruit, to be firstborn; the clan is called the Bachrites.
biblical_def: Two men bear this name. The first is the second son of Benjamin, named among the household of seventy souls that went down into Egypt with Jacob: the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard (Gen 46:21). Chronicles gives his house in full — nine sons, all heads of fathers' houses among mighty men of valour (1Ch 7:6, 8). The second is a son of Ephraim, head of the family of the Bachrites in the wilderness census (Num 26:35). The name means a young camel, and behind it stands bakar, the verb of bearing early — the root of bekor, the firstborn, and of bikkurim, the firstfruits. Israel's whole sacrificial calendar turned on that idea: the first of the flock, the first of the harvest, the first of the womb all belonged to the LORD by right, and were rendered before the rest was touched. It is a name that says, in one word, who gets the first claim.
webster_summary: The name of two men: the second son of Benjamin, and a son of Ephraim who headed the family of the Bachrites. It means a young camel, or firstborn.
webster_full: BECHER, Hebrew Beker, a young camel, or firstborn.

2. A son of Ephraim, head of the family of the Bachrites.
From bakar, to bear early, the root of firstborn and of firstfruits.

corruption_summary: Giving is treated as what may be spared after everything else; the firstfruits principle puts God's portion first, before the rest is touched.
corruption_paragraphs: The ordinary practice, in churches as much as anywhere, is to meet obligations, cover costs, allow for comfort, and give out of whatever survives the month. Scripture inverts the order and makes a doctrine of it. Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase (Pro 3:9). The sheaf was waved before the harvest was eaten; the firstling of the flock was the LORD's before the flock was counted; and Abel's offering was accepted because it was the firstlings and the fat, while Cain brought simply of the fruit of the ground (Gen 4:3-4).

The reason is not that God is short of resources; every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills (Psa 50:10). It is that what a man puts first reveals what he actually believes, and that giving from the top of the income is an act of faith about the rest of it, while giving from the bottom is an act of arithmetic. Malachi's challenge is the only one of its kind in Scripture: bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse… and prove me now herewith (Mal 3:10). The principle to recover is order rather than amount — the first claim is God's, and a man who settles that question in advance has settled a great many others with it.
